say.text: A 19-year-old has had central abdominal pain for 12 hours, and it is now worse. Before I explain anything, take a guess.
Which course is typical for his pain?

choices.label: Right iliac fossa pain that later spreads to the umbilicus
Periumbilical colicky pain that later shifts to the right iliac fossa
Constant right iliac fossa pain from the start that never moves
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the first sensation. The gut's own nerves are central and vague.
Which layer has to be inflamed before pain can point to one spot?
Starting in the right iliac fossa feels right, because that is where the pain ends up. It is tempting for that reason.
But early pain is visceral and central, from T10 (K26). It localises to the right iliac fossa only once the parietal peritoneum is involved (K27).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at the order: the end point of the story is not its start.

say.text: Constant pain from the start is tempting: the right iliac fossa is the picture you remember from the ward, so it feels like the first picture too.
But the early pain is periumbilical and colicky (K30). It shifts to the right iliac fossa later (K5).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: the classic pain starts in the middle and moves.

say.text: Yes. The pain starts periumbilical and colicky, then shifts to the right iliac fossa.
Here is the chain, one link at a time. Luminal obstruction starts it. Mucus keeps coming, so the pressure inside rises.
Venous congestion comes next, then arterial compromise. The appendicular artery is an end artery, so gangrene and then perforation follow.
The pain is now sharp and sits over the right iliac fossa. Why does it localise there, and not earlier?

choices.label: Rising lumen pressure over-stimulates T10 afferents directly
Inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, giving localised pain
Wall ischaemia starts before the lumen is blocked
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which layer of peritoneum can feel touch and point to a spot?
Does the visceral layer do that, or does something else?
Rising pressure is tempting: it causes the pain, so it feels like it should also decide where the pain sits.
But the T10 visceral signal stays central and diffuse, however strong it gets (K26). What is right is the parietal peritoneum, which localises the pain (K27).

sure_note.text: You were sure. Pressure explains why it hurts, not where it hurts.

say.text: Ischaemia first is tempting: gangrene is the end picture you remember, so it feels like the start of the story.
But the wall is starved only after the lumen blocks, the pressure rises and venous return fails (K24, K25).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the order: ischaemia comes after the pressure, not before the block.

say.text: Yes. Once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, the pain turns somatic and sits over the right iliac fossa.
Typical appendicitis gives three symptoms. Which order do they come in?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the first symptom the inflamed gut produces, the one you feel before anything else.
Then ask what comes after it.
Vomiting first is tempting: it opens gastroenteritis and many obstructions, so it feels like the usual start here too.
In appendicitis pain comes first, and vomiting follows it (K6). Vomiting is only a few episodes after the pain starts (K31).

sure_note.text: You were sure. Vomiting that comes first points away from appendicitis.

say.text: Fever first is tempting: fever is the sign people look for, so it feels like it should open the story.
In typical appendicitis the fever is low-grade and comes after the pain and vomiting (K6, K32).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: a high fever early in the story points away from the typical course.

say.text: Yes. Pain comes first, then vomiting, then low-grade fever (K6, K32).
An 8-year-old had a viral illness last week and now has right iliac fossa pain. What is the commonest cause of the luminal block?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the age in the stem first.
What sits in a child's appendix wall that shrinks as the child grows older?
Faecolith is tempting: it is the cause every textbook names, and it feels like the default answer.
But the age decides it. In a child the usual block is lymphoid hyperplasia, often after a viral illness (K14). A faecolith is the adult cause (K15).

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age first: the cause changes with it.

say.text: Yes. Lymphoid hyperplasia, often after a viral illness, is the commonest block in children (K14).
A 45-year-old has had right iliac fossa pain for three days. What is the commonest cause of the luminal block at this age?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go back to the age: the child's answer may not carry over.
What hardens and collects in an older lumen, and what does the wall's lymphoid tissue do with age?
Lymphoid hyperplasia is tempting: it was the answer a minute ago, so the child case is still fresh.
But lymphoid tissue shrinks with age, so in adults a faecolith is the usual block (K15, K95).

sure_note.text: You were sure. The same cause can flip with the age in the stem.

say.text: Yes. In adults a faecolith is the commonest block, and its presence raises the risk of perforation (K15).
